steps.say: A catheter is a highway for bacteria in both directions, and infections climb it by two distinct routes. The extraluminal route creeps up outside the tube as a living biofilm between catheter and urethral wall, while the intraluminal route swims up inside after the drainage bag or its tap gets contaminated. Closed sterile drainage blocks the inner road, but only early removal closes the outer one.
steps.tx: Prevent **CAUTI** (catheter infection, catheter-associated urinary tract infection) by blocking both ascents: **extraluminal biofilm** (bacterial slime creeping along the catheter-urethral interface) migration outside the tube, and **intraluminal ascension** (germ swim upwards) inside after **drainage bag contamination** (dirty bag or tap). Keep the closed sterile circuit unbroken below bladder level, and remove the catheter the hour it is no longer needed, because dwell time drives every infection.

vis.alt: Diagram of three-way Foley catheter showing triple lumens for irrigation and drainage.
vis.caption: Three-way Foley catheter: closed sterile drainage blocks intraluminal ascent. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Every extra catheter day buys measurable bacteriuria, and the arithmetic is brutal. The risk climbs by 3 to 7 percent per day of indwelling drainage, so by 30 days of continuous catheterization nearly 100 percent of urines grow bacteria. Bacteriuria is not always infection, but the biofilm reservoir behind it seeds bloodstream invasion, which is why nurse led removal reminders save lives.
steps.tx: Count the cost of delay: **bacteriuria accumulation** (daily germ build-up) rises **3% to 7%** (three to seven in a hundred) per day of **indwelling catheter** (tube left inside) drainage, nearing **100%** (all patients) by **30 days** (thirty days) of continuous use. Daily review with stop orders and nurse led removal prompts is therefore infection control, not paperwork, because each spared day deletes its slice of sepsis risk.

steps.say: Sometimes the natural channel is barred and the bladder must be reached through the belly wall. Suprapubic cystostomy drains through a stab above the pubis when urethral catheterization is impossible or forbidden: acute bacterial prostatitis where a catheter seeds infection, traumatic urethral disruption where it completes the tear, and severe stricture where it builds a false passage. Choosing the belly route in these three saves the urethra for later repair.
steps.tx: Divert to **suprapubic cystostomy** (belly wall bladder drain) for retention with a **contraindicated urethral catheter** (urethral route forbidden) setting: acute bacterial prostatitis (catheter spreads infection), traumatic urethral disruption (catheter completes the tear), and severe urethral stricture (catheter bores false passages). The suprapubic tube rests the injured urethra for months while definitive reconstruction is planned.

vis.alt: Suprapubic cystostomy catheter set with trocar and split sheath cannula.
vis.caption: Suprapubic cystostomy set: belly route when the urethral route is forbidden. Credit: James Heilman, MD.

steps.say: The suprapubic stab is blind only when the surgeon makes it so, and the bowel pays for arrogance. Percutaneous puncture is permitted solely when the bladder stands palpably distended above the pubis or sits pinned under real time ultrasound. A flat empty bladder is concealed behind bowel loops, and a trocar through them is followed by faecal peritonitis from a preventable small bowel perforation.
steps.tx: Attempt **percutaneous puncture** (needle stab drainage) only with a palpably distended bladder or accurate **ultrasound guidance** (real-time scan localisation), because blind stabbing risks fatal **bowel perforation** (trocar through small bowel). Feel the dome above the pubis or watch the needle enter urine on screen; if neither confirms a full bladder, place the catheter under direct vision in theatre instead.

steps.say: The enlarged prostate lifts the bladder neck into a hill that straight catheters ram and fail. The Coude tip catheter, also called Tiemann, bends its tip 45 degrees upward like a finger pointing to the ceiling, sliding over the raised neck and the median lobe hump. One gentle pass with the curve up succeeds where repeated straight stabs only dig false tunnels.
steps.tx: Negotiate the raised neck with the **Coude-tip catheter** (**Tiemann**, bent tip catheter) whose **45-degree** (forty five degree) anterior curve rides over elevated bladder necks and enlarged prostate **median lobe** (middle obstructing hump) without false passages. Advance slowly with the tip pointing to twelve o clock and never force against resistance, because the bent tip finds the true channel that straight catheters miss.

steps.say: A balloon that will not come down traps the catheter inside the patient, and panic pulling tears the urethra. Work the deflation ladder calmly: cut the inflation arm to release valve blockage, thread a fine stylet down the channel to pierce the inner valve, then burst the balloon under transabdominal ultrasound guidance, and finally aspirate it with a transrectal or transvaginal needle. Each rung is kinder than a forced pull.
steps.tx: Climb the **balloon deflation failure** (stuck inflated balloon) ladder stepwise: cut the inflation arm, pass a fine stylet through the channel, **ultrasound-guided puncture** (scan watched bursting) of the balloon, or transrectal and transvaginal needle aspiration. Forced traction ruptures the urethra, so exhaust every rung first, and confirm complete deflation on scan before withdrawing the catheter gently.

steps.say: Coated catheters promise fewer germs, and the promise is only half kept. Silver alloy and nitrofurazone impregnated antimicrobial catheters trim short term asymptomatic bacteriuria on the ward, but trials show no consistent fall in clinical sepsis or death. Buy them for short stays if budgets allow, but never let a fancy coating excuse leaving the tube in an extra day.
steps.tx: Weigh **antimicrobial catheters** (germ fighting tubes): **silver alloy** (silver coated) and nitrofurazone-impregnated models reduce short-term asymptomatic bacteriuria in hospital, yet have not consistently reduced clinical sepsis or overall mortality. Coating supplements but never substitutes removal: the cheapest infection control remains the earliest possible catheter exit, coated or plain.

steps.say: A bladder that squeezes against its own catheter cramps painfully and leaks around the tube, mimicking blockage. These catheter induced spasms settle with anticholinergic therapy such as solifenacin or oxybutynin, or with beta-3 agonists that relax the detrusor, alongside checking that the balloon sits in the bladder and the tube drains freely. Never upsize the catheter for spasms, because a bigger tube is followed by a bigger squeeze.
steps.tx: Calm **catheter-induced bladder spasms** (cramping against the tube) with **anticholinergic therapy** (**solifenacin**, **oxybutynin**) or beta-3 agonists that quiet the detrusor, after verifying balloon position and drainage patency. Spasms with leakage around the tube signal irritation, not blockage, so resist upsizing: a larger catheter provokes stronger cramps while the true fix is relaxation plus correct placement.
